title: Built While Running
endLine: A brain makes extra while it runs, then selects what stays.

scenes.tts: Branches that fire with their neighbours tend to stay. The genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest. But measuring needs a working circuit. Does a brain wait until it is finished to switch on?
scenes.narration: Branches that fire with their neighbours tend to stay. The genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest. But measuring needs a working circuit. Does a brain wait until it is finished to switch on?
scenes.caption: Branches that fire with their neighbours tend to stay. The genome stores rules, and the tissue measures the rest. But measuring needs a working circuit. Does a brain wait until it is finished to switch on?
scenes.visual: COLOUR MAP carried from the first film: YELLOW neurons, axons and synapse dots; GREY anatomy and axes; GREEN activity flashes; RED removal (fading, retracting, dying); TEAL rules; BLUE genome. New in this film: WHITE age scrubber; pale GOLD drops for target support; MAGENTA auditory cortex; CORAL prefrontal cortex. THE WORLD, kept all film: LEFT 45% of the frame, a large rounded 'cortex window' (GREY outline, about 65% of frame height) showing a magnified patch of cortex: a dozen YELLOW neurons with branching arbors, small YELLOW dots where branches meet (synapses), GREEN flashes running along branches as cells fire. RIGHT 50%, a plot: x axis 'age' with ticks birth, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30 years (spacing compressed, schematic); y axis 'synapse density', no numbers, an 'adult' dashed GREY reference line. A WHITE scrubber on the age axis sets the age shown in the window: the window's synapse-dot count tracks the plot's curve at that age, and the window's outline grows slowly larger with age (tissue growth). A small 'schematic' tag sits at bottom right all film. Open on the first film's last picture: the tightened retinal map, endings in the position palette, GREEN flashes sweeping in step; a small BLUE DNA icon with a cross through a long list. On 'tissue measures the rest' the map dissolves into the cortex window at left, where YELLOW branches are still growing outward while GREEN flashes already run along the finished ones. On the question, an electronic circuit board slides in at right (GREY board, solder joints), its plug hanging loose and unplugged, with a soldering iron still at work. White text across the top: 'Switched on when finished?' Ambient motion: flashes keep running in the window; a thread of solder smoke drifts from the board.
Title 'Built While Running' fades in for 2 s above the two pictures while the question text fades out. GREEN flashes keep running in the cortex window; branches keep growing.

scenes.tts: An electronic circuit is assembled first, then switched on. Once it is finished, its wiring does not change with use. A developing neural circuit works while it is being built.
scenes.narration: An electronic circuit is assembled first, then switched on. Once it is finished, its wiring does not change with use. A developing neural circuit works while it is being built.
scenes.caption: An electronic circuit is assembled first, then switched on. Once it is finished, its wiring does not change with use. A developing neural circuit works while it is being built.
scenes.visual: Right: the soldering iron lifts away, the plug clicks in, and the board's traces light up; a tag 'assembled, then on' appears. The lit traces stay fixed; a tag 'wiring fixed' fades in beside them. On 'A developing neural circuit', the camera eases left to the cortex window, which brightens: some branches are still extending while others already carry GREEN flashes. Tag under the window: 'working while built'.

scenes.tts: Embryonic neurons fire. Connections made early carry signals while later ones are still growing. Those signals, and later experience, help decide which connections stay.
scenes.narration: Embryonic neurons fire. Connections made early carry signals while later ones are still growing. Those signals, and later experience, help decide which connections stay.
scenes.caption: Embryonic neurons fire. Connections made early carry signals while later ones are still growing. Those signals, and later experience, help decide which connections stay.
scenes.visual: The circuit board slides out for good; the plot appears at right, empty, with its axes and the WHITE scrubber parked before 'birth'. In the window: on 'Embryonic neurons fire', GREEN flashes. On 'made early', the older, thicker branches carry repeated GREEN flashes; on 'still growing', thin new branch tips creep outward with no flashes yet. On 'help decide which connections stay', a few synapse dots on often-flashing branches brighten and thicken; one dot on a silent branch dims toward RED (it is not removed yet).

scenes.tts: The same rule, overproduce then select, works on whole neurons. Development makes more neurons than the finished circuit keeps, and many of them die.
scenes.narration: The same rule, overproduce then select, works on whole neurons. Development makes more neurons than the finished circuit keeps, and many of them die.
scenes.caption: The same rule, overproduce then select, works on whole neurons. Development makes more neurons than the finished circuit keeps, and many of them die.
scenes.visual: A TEAL card slides in over the top of the window: 'overproduce, then select'. The window re-centres on a simpler scene in the same frame: a row of eight YELLOW neurons at left sends axons right to a GREY band of target tissue labelled 'target'. On 'more neurons than the finished circuit keeps', the row fills to fourteen neurons, crowding the target. On 'many of them die', several neurons turn RED and fade away (schematic count, no number on screen).

scenes.tts: Which ones live is shaped by competition. Targets supply limited support, such as nerve growth factor, and the neurons compete for it.
scenes.narration: Which ones live is shaped by competition. Targets supply limited support, such as nerve growth factor, and the neurons compete for it.
scenes.caption: Which ones live is shaped by competition. Targets supply limited support, such as nerve growth factor, and the neurons compete for it.
scenes.visual: Rewind the row to fourteen neurons. The GREY target releases a small, fixed supply of pale GOLD drops, labelled 'nerve growth factor'. The drops travel back along some axons and gather in those cell bodies, which brighten. Neurons that receive few drops turn RED and fade, leaving the same survivors as in s04. Tag at top: 'competition for support'. Survivors keep GREEN flashing.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. A brain does not wait to be finished. It runs while it is built. It makes extra, and what stays is decided after the connections form.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. A brain does not wait to be finished. It runs while it is built. It makes extra, and what stays is decided after the connections form.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. A brain does not wait to be finished. It runs while it is built. It makes extra, and what stays is decided after the connections form.
scenes.visual: The window returns to the cortex patch (YELLOW arbors, synapse dots, GREEN flashes). The TEAL card sits above it. Three short lines appear in turn under the window on the matching words, each in TEXT colour: 'runs while built', 'makes extra', 'selection after connections'. On 'makes extra', extra branches and dots sprout across the window; on 'what stays is decided', the often-flashing ones brighten while a few silent ones dim RED and retract.

scenes.tts: If the human cortex works this way, synapses should rise, then fall. In 1979, Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses per unit volume in human frontal cortex, from people of many ages.
scenes.narration: If the human cortex works this way, synapses should rise, then fall. In 1979, Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses per unit volume in human frontal cortex, from people of many ages.
scenes.caption: If the human cortex works this way, synapses should rise, then fall. In 1979, Peter Huttenlocher counted synapses per unit volume in human frontal cortex, from people of many ages.
scenes.visual: The three lines and the TEAL card fade. On 'rise, then fall', a faint dashed YELLOW arc sketches up and down across the plot, then vanishes (a guess, not data). Label in the window's corner: 'frontal cortex'. On 'counted synapses per unit volume', a small GREY counting cube appears inside the window and the synapse dots inside it blink once each as they are counted; tag on the plot's y axis brightens: 'synapse density'. On 'many ages', a row of small GREY sample ticks appears along the age axis. Tag at top: 'Huttenlocher, 1979'.

scenes.tts: Density was already high at birth. It rose through infancy and peaked at about one to two years, roughly half again the adult value. Then it declined through childhood and adolescence.
scenes.narration: Density was already high at birth. It rose through infancy and peaked at about 1 to 2 years, roughly half again the adult value. Then it declined through childhood and adolescence.
scenes.caption: Density was already high at birth. It rose through infancy and peaked at about 1 to 2 years, roughly half again the adult value. Then it declined through childhood and adolescence.
scenes.visual: Schematic curve, drawn in YELLOW as the WHITE scrubber travels right: relative density (adult = 1.0 on the dashed line) starts above the adult line at birth (about 1.1, schematic), rises to a peak of 1.5 between 1 and 2 years (the one value from the lesson: label 'peak ≈ 1.5 × adult'), then slopes down through 5 and 10 years and reaches the adult line by about 20 (schematic). The window tracks the scrubber: synapse dots crowd in toward the peak, then thin out, while the window's outline grows steadily larger with age. Small labels along the axis on the matching words: 'infancy', 'childhood', 'adolescence'.

scenes.tts: But the cortex itself keeps growing through childhood. So does a falling density, on its own, prove that synapses were lost?
scenes.narration: But the cortex itself keeps growing through childhood. So does a falling density, on its own, prove that synapses were lost?
scenes.caption: But the cortex itself keeps growing through childhood. So does a falling density, on its own, prove that synapses were lost?
scenes.visual: The scrubber rests at 10 years. On 'keeps growing', the window outline pulses as it enlarges a little further; the counting cube inside stays the same size. Question card in white across the top: 'Does falling density prove loss?' The curve and the growing window stay on screen; no answer is shown.
Predict pause. The question card stays. GREEN flashes keep running in the window; the window outline breathes slowly; nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: Not by itself. A falling density could partly reflect tissue growth. It fits synapse loss without proving it, and it cannot show what decided which synapses stayed. Studies in animals that follow the same dendritic spines over time show the loss directly.
scenes.narration: Not by itself. A falling density could partly reflect tissue growth. It fits synapse loss without proving it, and it cannot show what decided which synapses stayed. Studies in animals that follow the same dendritic spines over time show the loss directly.
scenes.caption: Not by itself. A falling density could partly reflect tissue growth. It fits synapse loss without proving it, and it cannot show what decided which synapses stayed. Studies in animals that follow the same dendritic spines over time show the loss directly.
scenes.visual: Question card dissolves. Split the window in two side by side, both the same enlarged size, each with the same counting cube: LEFT, the same synapse dots as before spread apart as the window stretches, so fewer fall inside the cube (tag 'growth: same synapses'); RIGHT, some dots turn RED and vanish (tag 'loss: fewer synapses'). Both cubes show the same lower count. On 'what decided', a small RED question mark appears over the right half. On 'follow the same dendritic spines over time', the split closes into one window showing a single YELLOW dendrite with a row of spines, imaged at three time points one under another (tag 'same spines, over time'); some spines present at the first time point are gone at the last.

scenes.tts: The timing also differs between regions. In one study, auditory cortex peaked at about three months, and prefrontal cortex after fifteen months. Another found prefrontal spine loss continuing into the third decade of life.
scenes.narration: The timing also differs between regions. In one study, auditory cortex peaked at about 3 months, and prefrontal cortex after 15 months. Another found prefrontal spine loss continuing into the third decade of life.
scenes.caption: The timing also differs between regions. In one study, auditory cortex peaked at about 3 months, and prefrontal cortex after 15 months. Another found prefrontal spine loss continuing into the third decade of life.
scenes.visual: Back to the full world. The YELLOW frontal curve dims to a ghost. Two schematic curves are drawn over it on the same age axis: MAGENTA labelled 'auditory', peaking at about 3 months (a tick marked '3 mo' appears between birth and 1); CORAL labelled 'prefrontal', peaking after 15 months (tick '15 mo'). Peak heights are not data: both are drawn to the same height. On 'third decade of life', the CORAL curve's tail extends and keeps sloping down past 20 toward 30 years; a CORAL bracket over 20 to 30 labelled 'still losing spines'. The window shows the scrubber at 25: a few synapse dots still dimming RED.

scenes.tts: Selection is one part of a longer build. The course follows nine overlapping steps, from induction to refinement. Selection is most on show in two of them: naturally occurring death, and activity-dependent refinement.
scenes.narration: Selection is one part of a longer build. The course follows nine overlapping steps, from induction to refinement. Selection is most on show in two of them: naturally occurring death, and activity-dependent refinement.
scenes.caption: Selection is one part of a longer build. The course follows nine overlapping steps, from induction to refinement. Selection is most on show in two of them: naturally occurring death, and activity-dependent refinement.
scenes.visual: The region curves fade. Across the plot area, nine GREY bars appear as a schematic, overlapping staircase (each bar starts before the previous one ends), labelled only at the ends: '1 induction' at left, '9 refinement' at right. Tag: 'overlapping steps, schematic'. On 'naturally occurring death', bar 7 lights TEAL with label '7 neuron death'; a tiny echo of the RED fading neurons from s04 flickers on it. On 'activity-dependent refinement', bar 9 lights TEAL; the window beside it shows GREEN flashes and a RED branch retracting.

scenes.tts: So a brain is not a board, soldered and then plugged in. It is a circuit already at work, built with extra, and trimmed as it runs.
scenes.narration: So a brain is not a board, soldered and then plugged in. It is a circuit already at work, built with extra, and trimmed as it runs.
scenes.caption: So a brain is not a board, soldered and then plugged in. It is a circuit already at work, built with extra, and trimmed as it runs.
scenes.visual: The staircase fades. A faint ghost of the plugged-in circuit board appears at right for 'not a board', then dissolves. On 'already at work', the cortex window fills more of the frame, GREEN flashes running; on 'built with extra', a burst of extra branches and synapse dots sprouts; on 'trimmed as it runs', the silent ones dim RED and retract while the flashing ones stay bright. The frontal YELLOW curve on the plot re-brightens in step: up, then down.
End card over the dimmed but still moving cortex window (GREEN flashes keep running). Large white text, centred: 'A brain makes extra while it runs, then selects what stays.'
